title: Kabir in the Granth
hook: a Sikh reads aloud from the Guru Granth Sahib, and the line is signed: says Kabir
tomorrow: who did Kabir mock hardest? his own people were on the list.

segments.voice: Yesterday, only flowers: Kabir's followers fought over his body and found flowers to share. Today, the week comes back around, and a weaver's songs turn up inside someone else's scripture.
screen: `ONLY FLOWERS.` → `A WEAVER IN SOMEONE ELSE'S BOOK.`

segments.voice: Theo said yes. He'll read at Hannah's wedding, the passage she picked, and he's been practicing it out loud in the car. Somewhere this morning, in a gurdwara, a Sikh reader is doing the same thing, reading aloud from the Guru Granth Sahib. And partway through, the line is signed with a name that isn't a Guru's at all: says Kabir. So how did the weaver get in?
screen: `THEO SAYS YES.` → `A READER IN A GURDWARA.` → `SIGNED: SAYS KABIR.`

segments.voice: Sikh tradition tells it this way. Guru Arjan gathered the hymns of the Gurus before him into one book, the Adi Granth. And he went further. He gathered the songs of bhagats, saints from outside the Sikh line: Kabir the weaver, Farid the Sufi, Namdev, Ravidas. He set their hymns in the same ragas as the Gurus' own, and near the end of the book comes a long run of Kabir's saloks, his short sayings. Where the Gurus saw a thing differently, they didn't cut Kabir out. They wrote their own couplet beside his. Here's the teaching. Sikhs honor that book as the Guru itself, the Guru Granth Sahib: carried in with care, opened each morning, read and sung. So a weaver's words are bowed to as part of the Guru. Now the week, back around. The weaver, claimed by three houses. God beside you, as near as breath. The swing of every world. None worse than me. The moon inside every body. Only flowers. And today: in the Granth.
screen: `GURU ARJAN GATHERS THE HYMNS.` · `THE BHAGATS: KABIR, FARID, NAMDEV, RAVIDAS.` · `A COUPLET BESIDE HIS, NOT A CUT.` · `THE BOOK HONORED AS GURU.` · then, large: `IN THE GRANTH.`

segments.voice: Copy one Kabir line from this week by hand: beside you, or none worse than me, or the moon inside. Write it slowly, and sign it the way the Granth does: Kabir. Then sit with the page in front of you.
Kabir in the Granth: a weaver's hymns and sayings, set beside the Gurus' own in the book Sikhs honor as Guru.
Here's the line: in the granth. A weaver's words, bowed to as part of the Guru. A week with Kabir, nearly done.
